Neonates of Notothenia rossii emerge from the demersal egg with a total length of just 1.51 centimeters [Lb = 1.51 centimeters], a remarkably small size given the considerable ultimate length this species can achieve. Field surveys of the Scotia Arc have documented that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, still relying on endogenous reserves, possess a wet weight of approximately 0.025 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.025 grams], reflecting a period of lecithotrophic dependence before the onset of exogenous feeding. This initial mass places them well within the range observed for other nototheniids, although the subsequent growth trajectory is notably steep. The species is iteroparous, and at the ambient temperature of 2.1 °C [T = 2.1 °C] that dominates its Southern Ocean habitat, mature females exhibit an annual reproductive output of approximately 37,000 eggs [Ri = annual reproductive output of approximately 37,000 eggs], typically released during a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year], a fecundity that reflects the substantial energetic investment in pelagic offspring.

As individuals progress through the pelagic larval phase and undergo larval metamorphosis, their growth is strongly influenced by the persistently cold conditions of the Southern Ocean, routinely measured at 2.1 °C [T = 2.1 °C]. Following the pelagic-benthic transition, post-settlement juveniles begin a period of accelerated mass gain, eventually reaching a wet weight at puberty of 2,350 grams [Wwp = 2,350 grams] for females, a mass that typically coincides with the onset of vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence. This value is derived from allometric relationships linking length to weight and marks a critical physiological threshold. The ultimate total length recorded for this species is 92 centimeters [Li = 92 centimeters], a maximum reported in museum specimen series from the Kerguelen Plateau, corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 9,700 grams [Wwi = approximately 9,700 grams] for fully grown adults. This size dimorphism is modest compared to some other nototheniids, but the associated mass accumulation is substantial.

Female Notothenia rossii attain sexual maturity at a total length of 58.5 centimeters [Lp = 58.5 centimeters], a metric recorded in multiple population surveys from the South Orkney Islands. This length, typically reached between 6 and 8 years following the pelagic larval phase, defines the size at which the first spawning event becomes biologically feasible. Delaying reproductive activation until this size allows females to allocate sufficient resources to a single large clutch; each spawning adult produces approximately 37,000 eggs per reproductive event [N_R_i = approximately 37,000 eggs per reproductive event], and given the species produces a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], the lifetime reproductive output can be considerable. The gonadosomatic index increases sharply at this length, reflecting a transition from somatic growth to investment in gamete production, a pattern common among slow-growing high-latitude teleosts.

The maximum lifespan documented for Notothenia rossii in the wild is approximately 5,475 days [am = approximately 5,475 days] at a habitat temperature of 2.1 °C [T = 2.1 °C], a value equivalent to about 15 years, though the oldest individuals are typically found in the most stable, least disturbed regions of the Antarctic continental shelf. This longevity, paired with the cold temperatures of its habitat, is consistent with the extended lifespans observed in other nototheniid species. During the post-reproductive phase, senescent adults gradually lose body condition, and natural mortality is often preceded by a period of diminished feeding activity. Comparative analyses indicate that this lifespan is near the upper end of the nototheniid range, potentially linked to the species' iteroparous breeding strategy and the low metabolic demands of the polar environment.

The life history strategy of Notothenia rossii, characterized by slow growth and deferred reproduction, is an adaptation to the extreme seasonality and low productivity of Antarctic waters. Reaching sexual maturity at 58.5 centimeters [Lp = 58.5 centimeters] of total length and an associated body mass of 2,350 grams [Wwp = 2,350 grams] allows females to attain a size sufficient to support the energetic demands of a single, massive annual clutch. This contrasts with many temperate marine fishes that mature earlier and smaller but produce multiple clutches within a year. The ultimate adult mass of 9,700 grams [Wwi = 9,700 grams] is among the highest recorded for any nototheniid, reflecting the species' occupation of a relatively productive niche within the otherwise oligotrophic Southern Ocean ecosystem. The lifespan of over 5,475 days [am = 5,475 days] further underscores the premium placed on adult survivorship in this environment at a temperature of 2.1 °C [T = 2.1 °C].
